title: Salt
deck: All life depends on it, and for most of history it was hard to get. Ten places where salt made towns, roads, taxes and a revolution in how to protest.
kidDeck: Everyone needs salt, and once it was hard to find. Visit ten places where salt made people rich, built roads and even helped a country win its freedom.

stops.title: A town built on brine
stops.text: Solnitsata, "the Saltworks", near today's Provadia in Bulgaria, is the oldest salt production centre in continental Europe, at work from 5500 to 4200 BC. Its population has been estimated at only 350, yet it was a fortified stone settlement. A great collection of gold found nearby, at Varna, has led archaeologists to think the salt trade made the town wealthy.
stops.kid: More than 7,000 years ago, people in what is now Bulgaria made salt and traded it. Their little town had stone walls. Lots of gold was found nearby, so the salt probably made them rich.

stops.title: The salt miners of Hallstatt
stops.text: Hallstatt, in the Austrian Alps, has produced salt since prehistoric times. By the Bronze Age it was a day-to-day commercial activity, carried out in large quantities and highly organised. The place gave its name to the Hallstatt culture of early Iron Age Europe, about 800 to 450 BC.
stops.kid: In the mountains of Austria, people have dug salt out of the rock since before history was written down. The village of Hallstatt became so important that a whole period of Europe's past is named after it.

stops.title: Rome's salt road
stops.text: The Via Salaria, the Salt Road, ran from Rome 242 km to the Adriatic coast. It owes its name to the Latin word for salt: it was the route by which the Sabines came to fetch salt from the marshes at the mouth of the Tiber. Some historians consider the road and its salt trade to be the origin of the settlement of Rome.
stops.kid: One of the oldest roads out of Rome is called the Salt Road. People used it to fetch salt from the marshes by the sea. Some historians think Rome grew up where it did because of this salt trade.

stops.title: The first salt tax
stops.text: Salt was first taxed in China, where salt taxation dates back to 300 BC. Taxing salt became one of the longest-standing sources of revenue for governments everywhere, because nobody can do without it. The pin sits on Zigong in Sichuan, a city formed from two old towns whose names mean "self-flow well" and "offering well", and where percussion drilling was developed.
stops.kid: Because everyone needs salt, rulers found they could make people pay a tax on it. China did this first, about 2,300 years ago. The pin is on a Chinese city famous for its deep salt wells.

stops.title: Chapels carved in salt
stops.text: At Wieliczka near Kraków, salt was made from brine springs from Neolithic times. The mine itself, excavated from the 13th century, produced table salt continuously until 1996. Underground are a lake, four chapels and many statues that miners carved out of the rock salt. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
stops.kid: This salt mine in Poland was worked for about 700 years. Deep underground the miners carved whole chapels and statues out of salt. You can visit them today.

stops.title: Salt in the Sahara
stops.text: Taghaza, in a salt pan in the desert of northern Mali, was an important source of rock salt for West Africa until the end of the 16th century. The traveller Ibn Battuta arrived there in 1352 after a 25-day journey from Sijilmasa, on his way to the Mali Empire. He found no trees, only sand. An earlier writer recorded that the salt was mined by enslaved people and carried south by a caravan that came once a year.
stops.kid: In the middle of the Sahara desert there was a village where salt was dug out of the ground. The diggers were enslaved people. A caravan carried the salt south. A famous traveller, Ibn Battuta, came here in 1352.

stops.title: The hated gabelle
stops.text: In France the gabelle was a state monopoly on the salt trade, and in some regions a salt tax. It was set up in the mid-14th century and lasted, with brief lapses, until 1946. It was very unpopular: it touched every French household, which needed salt for cooking, preserving food, making cheese and raising livestock.
stops.kid: In France, for hundreds of years, only the king's government was allowed to sell salt, and it charged a lot. People hated this rule, which was called the gabelle.

stops.title: A mountain of pink salt
stops.text: The Khewra Salt Mine in the Punjab, in today's Pakistan, is the world's second largest. Its history is said to go back to its discovery by Alexander's troops in 326 BC, though it began trading only in the Mughal era. It is famous for its pink salt.
stops.kid: This huge salt mine in Pakistan is the second biggest in the world. The story goes that soldiers of Alexander the Great found the salt more than 2,300 years ago. The salt here is pink.

stops.title: Gandhi picks up a handful of salt
stops.text: In colonial India the British taxed salt and controlled its making. On 12 March 1930 Mahatma Gandhi set out from Sabarmati Ashram on a 24-day march of 387 km to the sea at Dandi, where on 6 April he made salt himself. It was an act of nonviolent civil disobedience and tax resistance.
stops.kid: When Britain ruled India, Indians were not allowed to make their own salt. In 1930 Mahatma Gandhi walked 387 kilometres to the sea, for 24 days, and made salt there. He broke the law on purpose, peacefully, to show that the law was unfair.

stops.title: The biggest salt flat on Earth
stops.text: The Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia is the largest salt flat in the world, about 10,582 square kilometres, at 3,656 m above sea level. Its crust is a source of salt and covers a pool of brine that is exceptionally rich in lithium: a metal used in batteries.
stops.kid: High in the mountains of Bolivia is the biggest salt flat in the world. Under the salt is salty water with lithium in it, which is used to make batteries.

title: Inventing writing
deck: Wedges in clay, cracks in bone, an alphabet of 22 letters, a script designed by a king and one by a man who could not read. Ten places where people worked out how to make speech visible.
kidDeck: How do you draw a word? People in different parts of the world found different answers. Visit ten places where writing was invented, lost, or read again.

stops.title: Wedges in clay
stops.text: Cuneiform is the earliest known writing system. It was developed to write Sumerian, the language of southern Mesopotamia, and is named for the wedge-shaped marks that form its signs. Before it, clay tokens had been used to record amounts of livestock and goods. The script stayed in use until the 1st century BC. The pin is on Uruk, one of the ancient cities of southern Mesopotamia.
stops.kid: The oldest writing we know was made by pressing little wedge shapes into wet clay. It began in the land that is now Iraq, where people first used clay tokens to count their sheep and grain.

stops.title: Labels for a king's tomb
stops.text: In 1998, clay labels from the time of a ruler called Scorpion I, of about the 33rd century BC, were recovered at Abydos. They belong to the beginnings of Egyptian writing. Hieroglyphs grew into a formal system with more than 1,000 distinct characters, mixing signs for ideas, words and sounds.
stops.kid: In Egypt, some of the earliest writing was found on little clay labels in a king's tomb. Later, Egyptian writing had more than a thousand different picture signs, called hieroglyphs.

stops.title: Questions carved on bone
stops.text: The oldest attested form of written Chinese dates to the late 2nd millennium BC. At Yin, the last Shang capital, diviners heated ox shoulder blades and turtle shells until they cracked, then read the cracks. The question and the interpretation were carved on the same bone.
stops.kid: The oldest Chinese writing is carved on ox bones and turtle shells. Kings asked a question, the bone was heated until it cracked, and the answer was read from the cracks. Then the question was carved on the bone.

stops.title: Twenty-two letters
stops.text: The Phoenicians, a seafaring people of city-states along the coast of today's Lebanon, wrote with one of the first alphabets: 22 letters, all consonants. It was the first script with a fixed writing direction. Its direct descendants include the Aramaic and the early Greek alphabets.
stops.kid: The Phoenicians were sailors and traders. Instead of hundreds of signs, they wrote with just 22 letters. The Greek alphabet came from theirs, and many other alphabets too.

stops.title: A king's boast in three languages
stops.text: On a cliff at Mount Behistun in western Iran, Darius the Great, who ruled from 522 to 486 BC, had a huge relief and a multilingual royal inscription carved. Because it says the same thing in several languages, it was important to the decipherment of cuneiform.
stops.kid: A Persian king named Darius had his story carved high on a cliff, in more than one language. Much later, this helped scholars work out how to read the old wedge-shaped writing.

stops.title: The stone that unlocked Egypt
stops.text: The Rosetta Stone carries a decree issued in 196 BC, written three times: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic script and in Ancient Greek. A French army officer, Pierre-François Bouchard, found it in July 1799, built into a fort near Rashid. With its help Jean-François Champollion deciphered hieroglyphs in the 1820s.
stops.kid: Nobody could read Egyptian hieroglyphs any more. Then in 1799 a stone was found with the same message written in three ways, one of them in Greek, which people could still read. Using it, a Frenchman named Champollion cracked the code.

stops.title: Glyphs in the rainforest
stops.text: The earliest inscriptions that are identifiably Maya date to the 3rd century BCE, at sites such as San Bartolo, north-east of Tikal in Guatemala. Maya writing stayed in use until the Spanish conquest. It is the only writing system of Mesoamerica that has been substantially deciphered.
stops.kid: The Maya of Central America invented their own writing, made of detailed picture signs called glyphs. People used it for nearly two thousand years. Today experts can read much of it again.

stops.title: An alphabet made by a king
stops.text: Korea had written with Chinese characters since antiquity, though they suited the Korean language poorly. King Sejong, who ruled Joseon from 1418 to 1450, is remembered for creating a native alphabet. It was announced around the end of 1443 and published in 1446 under the name Hunminjeongeum, "Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People".
stops.kid: Korean was hard to write with Chinese characters. So King Sejong had a new alphabet made, just for Korean. It was published in 1446 and Koreans still use it today. The pin is on Seoul, the capital of South Korea.

stops.title: Sequoyah's 85 signs
stops.text: Sequoyah, of the Cherokee Nation, could not read or write when he began. In 1821 he completed a syllabary for the Cherokee language, in which each of 85 symbols stands for a syllable. By 1825 the majority of Cherokees could read and write in it. That year New Echota, in today's Georgia, became the Cherokee capital.
stops.kid: Sequoyah was a Cherokee man who had never learned to read. He invented a way to write his own language all by himself, with 85 signs, one for each sound. Within a few years most Cherokee people could read and write.

stops.title: The tablets nobody can read
stops.text: On Easter Island, in the 19th century, outsiders came upon a system of glyphs called rongorongo that looks like writing. About two dozen inscribed wooden objects survive, scattered in museums. Many people have tried to decipher them. None has succeeded, and it is not even certain that it is true writing.
stops.kid: On Easter Island, far out in the Pacific Ocean, people carved rows of little signs into wooden boards. Only about two dozen of these boards are left. Nobody alive can read them.

title: Keepers of knowledge
deck: Clay tablets in Nineveh, scrolls in Alexandria, 81,352 wooden blocks on a Korean mountain, a trillion web pages in San Francisco. Eleven attempts to keep what people know.
kidDeck: How do you keep everything people know safe? Visit eleven great libraries, from clay tablets 2,700 years old to a library of the whole Internet.

stops.title: A king's 30,000 tablets
stops.text: Ashurbanipal, the last great king of the Assyrian Empire, gathered a library at Nineveh in the 7th century BCE. More than 30,000 clay tablets and fragments survive, with texts of all kinds in several languages, among them the Epic of Gilgamesh. Austen Henry Layard's excavations found them from late 1849, and most are now in the British Museum.
stops.kid: About 2,700 years ago a king named Ashurbanipal collected a huge library. His books were clay tablets, and more than 30,000 pieces survive. One of them holds one of the oldest stories in the world, about a hero called Gilgamesh.

stops.title: The Great Library
stops.text: The Library of Alexandria was one of the largest and most significant libraries of the ancient world, part of a research institution called the Mouseion, dedicated to the Muses. It may have been planned under Ptolemy I, but was probably not built until the reign of his son Ptolemy II. It quickly acquired many papyrus scrolls.
stops.kid: In the Egyptian city of Alexandria stood the most famous library of the ancient world. It was full of scrolls made of papyrus, and scholars came to live and study there.

stops.title: A library to save the Greeks
stops.text: The Imperial Library of Constantinople was the last of the great libraries of the ancient world. It was founded by the emperor Constantius II, who reigned from 337 to 361 and set up a scriptorium so that surviving Greek literature could be copied. It preserved the knowledge of the Greeks and Romans for almost 1,000 years, through fires and the crusader raids of 1204.
stops.kid: In Constantinople, an emperor set up a library where old Greek books were copied out again by hand so they would not be lost. It kept that knowledge safe for almost a thousand years.

stops.title: Nalanda
stops.text: Nalanda was a great Buddhist monastery in Magadha, today's Bihar, near the city of Rajgir. Established by the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I around 427 CE, it operated for almost a thousand years. It is widely considered one of the greatest centres of learning of the ancient world, and is often called the world's first residential university.
stops.kid: Nalanda, in India, was a huge Buddhist monastery where students lived and studied. It lasted almost a thousand years. People often call it the first university in the world where students lived on the campus.

stops.title: The House of Wisdom
stops.text: The House of Wisdom in Baghdad was a major academy and intellectual centre of the Abbasid era. Under the caliph al-Ma'mun, who reigned from 813 to 833, it became a public academy and library. It was destroyed in 1258 during the Mongol siege of Baghdad. How much it resembled a university is disputed: recent scholarship has challenged the picture of specialised departments and organised debate.
stops.kid: In Baghdad there was a great library and school called the House of Wisdom. Scholars gathered there to study. It was destroyed when the Mongols attacked the city in 1258.

stops.title: The cave of manuscripts
stops.text: In 1900 a wandering Daoist monk, Wang Yuanlu, discovered a great store of manuscripts at the Mogao Caves near Dunhuang, an oasis on the Silk Road. They are religious and secular texts in Chinese, Tibetan and other languages, on hemp, silk and paper. Wang sold many of them to Aurel Stein and Paul Pelliot for a modest sum.
stops.kid: In 1900 a monk found a great store of very old writings at a cave temple in China, on the old Silk Road. They were in many languages. He sold many of them to explorers from Europe.

stops.title: 81,352 wooden blocks
stops.text: The Tripitaka Koreana is the Buddhist scriptures carved onto 81,352 wooden printing blocks in the 13th century. It is the oldest intact version of the Chinese Buddhist canon. The blocks have been housed at the temple of Haeinsa, in the mountains of South Korea, since 1398.
stops.kid: In a temple in the mountains of Korea, there is a library made of wood. The Buddhist holy books were carved onto more than 80,000 wooden blocks, ready for printing. They have been kept there since 1398.

stops.title: Timbuktu's family libraries
stops.text: In Timbuktu, in northern Mali, a large number of manuscripts have been preserved for centuries in private households. They cover art, medicine, philosophy and science, along with copies of the Quran. Their dates range from the late 13th to the early 20th centuries.
stops.kid: In the desert city of Timbuktu, families have looked after old handwritten books for hundreds of years. The books are about medicine, the stars, art and religion.

stops.title: The Pope's library
stops.text: The Vatican Apostolic Library, the library of the Holy See, was formally established by Pope Sixtus IV on 15 June 1475.
stops.kid: The Pope's library in Rome was officially founded in 1475. It is one of the oldest libraries in the world.

stops.title: Oxford's Bodleian
stops.text: The Bodleian is the main research library of the University of Oxford. Founded in 1602 by Sir Thomas Bodley, it is one of the oldest libraries in Europe and holds over 13 million printed items. By law it is entitled to a copy of works published in the United Kingdom.
stops.kid: This library in Oxford, England, opened in 1602 and has more than 13 million printed things in it. By law, it can get a copy of every new book published in the country.

stops.title: A library of the Internet
stops.text: The Internet Archive is a non-profit library founded in 1996 by Brewster Kahle. Its mission is "universal access to all knowledge". Its web archive, the Wayback Machine, holds more than one trillion captures of web pages, and has been open to the public since 2001.
stops.kid: Web pages change and disappear. Since 1996 a library in San Francisco has been saving copies of them. It now holds more than a trillion saved pages, and anyone can look at them.

title: Fighting the invisible
deck: An enslaved man in Boston, a country doctor, a hand-washing rule in Vienna, a water pump in Soho, a mould in London. Ten places where people learned to beat infectious disease.
kidDeck: For most of history nobody knew what made people sick. Visit ten places where people worked it out, step by step, and wiped one terrible disease off the Earth.

stops.title: A letter from Constantinople
stops.text: In August 1716 Lady Mary Wortley Montagu went with her husband, the new British ambassador, to Constantinople. She is known for introducing and advocating smallpox inoculation in Britain after her return from Turkey. The method, variolation, used material taken from a smallpox patient in the hope of causing a mild but protective infection.
stops.kid: An English lady, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, travelled to Constantinople in 1716. When she came home she taught people in Britain a way to protect themselves from a deadly disease called smallpox, by giving them a mild case of it on purpose.

stops.title: What Onesimus knew
stops.text: Onesimus was an African man enslaved by the Boston clergyman Cotton Mather. In 1716 or shortly before, he described to Mather how he had been inoculated against smallpox in Africa. When an outbreak began in Boston in 1721, Mather used that knowledge to argue for inoculation. The method worked, at a price: 1 to 2 percent of those variolated died, against 30 percent of those who caught smallpox naturally.
stops.kid: Onesimus was an African man who was enslaved in Boston. He explained how people in his homeland protected themselves from smallpox. When the disease struck Boston in 1721, his knowledge helped to save lives.

stops.title: The first vaccine
stops.text: Edward Jenner, a physician born in Berkeley in Gloucestershire, created the smallpox vaccine, the world's first vaccine. The words vaccine and vaccination come from Variolae vaccinae, "pustules of the cow", his term for cowpox, which he used in the title of his Inquiry in 1798.
stops.kid: An English doctor named Edward Jenner made the world's first vaccine. It protected people from smallpox, and it came from cowpox, a disease of cows. The word "vaccine" comes from the Latin word for cow.

stops.title: Wash your hands
stops.text: At the Vienna General Hospital, the doctors' maternity wards had three times the death rate of the midwives' wards. In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis proposed that doctors wash their hands in a chlorinated lime solution. The death rate of mothers fell from 18 percent to less than 2 percent. He is remembered as the "saviour of mothers".
stops.kid: In a hospital in Vienna, many mothers were dying after having their babies. A doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis told the other doctors to wash their hands before touching a patient. Far fewer mothers died.

stops.title: The pump on Broad Street
stops.text: In 1854 cholera broke out around Broad Street in Soho, London. The physician John Snow traced it to one public water pump and argued that germ-contaminated water was the cause. He is considered one of the founders of modern epidemiology.
stops.kid: In 1854 many people in one part of London fell ill with a disease called cholera. Dr John Snow worked out that they had all drunk water from the same pump. The water was carrying the disease.

stops.title: Pasteur's institute
stops.text: Louis Pasteur, a French chemist and microbiologist, is renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation and pasteurisation, which is named after him. His vaccines for rabies and anthrax are credited with saving millions of lives. In Paris in 1887 he established the Pasteur Institute, which he directed for the rest of his life.
stops.kid: Louis Pasteur was a French scientist who studied germs. He made vaccines against two deadly diseases, rabies and anthrax. Pasteurisation is named after him.

stops.title: A mould that kills bacteria
stops.text: In 1928 the Scottish physician Alexander Fleming discovered that the mould Penicillium rubens produces a substance that kills bacteria. It was later named penicillin: the first antibiotic. He shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain for the discovery and its curative effect. The pin is on St Mary's Hospital in Paddington, at whose medical school Fleming had trained.
stops.kid: In 1928 a Scottish doctor, Alexander Fleming, noticed that a mould made something that killed germs. It was called penicillin, the first antibiotic.

stops.title: A vaccine given away
stops.text: Jonas Salk, a professor at the University of Pittsburgh from 1947, developed one of the first successful polio vaccines. When its success was made public in April 1955 he was hailed as a miracle worker. He chose not to patent the vaccine or seek any profit from it, so that it could be distributed as widely as possible.
stops.kid: Polio, once called infantile paralysis, was a feared disease. In 1955 the world learned that Dr Jonas Salk's vaccine worked. He did not try to make money from it, so that it could reach as many people as possible.

stops.title: The last case
stops.text: In October 1977 Ali Maow Maalin, a hospital cook in Merca, Somalia, was diagnosed with smallpox. He recovered. He was the last person known to have caught the naturally occurring disease, and none of his many contacts developed it. As recently as 1967 an estimated 15 million people a year had caught smallpox and two million had died. In May 1980 the World Health Organization certified it eradicated worldwide.
stops.kid: In 1977 a hospital cook in Somalia named Ali Maow Maalin caught smallpox. He got better. He was the last person ever to catch it naturally. After thousands of years, vaccines had wiped smallpox off the Earth.

stops.title: A malaria cure from herbal medicine
stops.text: Tu Youyou studied in Beijing and spent her career researching Chinese herbal medicine at the China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences. She discovered artemisinin, a treatment for malaria that has saved millions of lives in China, Southeast Asia, Africa and South America. In 2015 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
stops.kid: Malaria is a deadly disease. A Chinese scientist named Tu Youyou studied traditional herbal medicines and found a new cure for it. Her medicine has saved millions of lives. In 2015 she won a Nobel Prize.

title: Leaving the ground
deck: A paper-maker's balloon in 1783, 852 feet over the sand in 1903, a metal ball in orbit in 1957, footprints on the Moon in 1969. Ten places where people left the ground.
kidDeck: People dreamed of flying for thousands of years. Then, in less than 200 years, they went from a paper balloon to the Moon. Visit ten places where it happened.

stops.title: A balloon made by paper-makers
stops.text: Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier were paper manufacturers from Annonay in France. They invented the hot air balloon, and on 4 June 1783 flew one at Annonay in front of a group of local dignitaries. Later that year their balloon made the first confirmed piloted ascent by humans.
stops.kid: Two brothers who made paper invented the hot air balloon. They showed it off in their home town in France on 4 June 1783. A few months later, people went up in one for the first time.

stops.title: The flying man
stops.text: Otto Lilienthal was the first person to make well-documented, repeated, successful flights with gliders, from an artificial hill he built near Berlin and from the Rhinow Hills. He showed that heavier-than-air flight was real. On 9 August 1896 his glider stalled and he could not regain control.
stops.kid: Otto Lilienthal built gliders, wings with no engine, and flew them again and again from hills near Berlin. People called him "the flying man". In 1896 one of his gliders crashed.

stops.title: Four flights on one morning
stops.text: On 17 December 1903, about four miles south of Kitty Hawk in North Carolina, Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first sustained flights in a powered, controlled, heavier-than-air aircraft. They flew four times. The last flight covered 852 feet, 260 metres. Minutes later a gust wrecked the machine.
stops.kid: On 17 December 1903 the brothers Orville and Wilbur Wright flew the first real aeroplane, one with an engine that the pilot could steer. They flew it four times that day. The longest flight went 260 metres.

stops.title: Across the Channel
stops.text: In 1909 the French aviator Louis Blériot became world-famous by making the first aeroplane flight across the English Channel. It won him a prize of 1,000 pounds offered by the Daily Mail newspaper. He had paid for his aircraft with money made from manufacturing car headlamps.
stops.kid: In 1909 a Frenchman, Louis Blériot, flew an aeroplane across the sea between France and England. Nobody had done that before. A newspaper gave him a big prize.

stops.title: New York to Paris, alone
stops.text: On 20 May 1927 Charles Lindbergh took off from Long Island, New York, in the single-engine Spirit of St. Louis. He landed at Le Bourget in Paris 33 hours and 30 minutes later, after about 5,800 km: the first solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic. In 1932 Amelia Earhart became the first woman to fly the Atlantic solo and nonstop.
stops.kid: In 1927 Charles Lindbergh flew alone from New York to Paris without stopping. It took him 33 and a half hours. Five years later Amelia Earhart became the first woman to fly across the Atlantic Ocean alone.

stops.title: A ball that went beep
stops.text: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial Earth satellite, from the range now known as the Baikonur Cosmodrome. It was a polished metal sphere 58 cm across with four radio antennas. It sent a radio signal back to Earth for three weeks, until its batteries ran down.
stops.kid: On 4 October 1957 a rocket carried a shiny metal ball, 58 centimetres across, into space. It was called Sputnik, and it was the first thing people ever put in orbit around the Earth. It sent radio signals for three weeks.

stops.title: The first people in orbit
stops.text: On 12 April 1961 the capsule Vostok 1 was launched from Baikonur with the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin aboard. It was the first human orbital spaceflight in history. On 16 June 1963 Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space. She orbited the Earth 48 times and spent almost three days in space, alone.
stops.kid: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first person to fly around the Earth in space. Two years later Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space. She went around the Earth 48 times, all by herself.

stops.title: To the Moon
stops.text: Apollo 11 was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed in the Sea of Tranquility on 20 July 1969 and spent more than 21 hours on the surface, while Michael Collins stayed in lunar orbit. Launch operations for the Apollo programme were carried out at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
stops.kid: In July 1969 three astronauts flew from Florida to the Moon. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed and walked on it. Michael Collins waited for them in the spaceship, circling the Moon. Then they flew back to Earth.

stops.title: A telescope a million and a half kilometres away
stops.text: On 25 December 2021 the James Webb Space Telescope was launched on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou in French Guiana. In January 2022 it arrived about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth. It is the largest telescope in space and observes in infrared, so it can see objects too old, distant or faint for the Hubble Space Telescope.
stops.kid: On Christmas Day 2021 a rocket launched the biggest telescope ever sent into space. It flew 1.5 million kilometres from Earth. It can see things that are too far away and too faint for any telescope before it.

stops.title: India lands near the Moon's south pole
stops.text: Chandrayaan-3, built by India's space agency ISRO, was launched on 14 July 2023 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota, an island off India's east coast. It carried a lander, Vikram, and a rover, Pragyan. On 23 August 2023 it touched down near the lunar south pole, at 69 degrees south.
stops.kid: In July 2023 India launched a spacecraft to the Moon from an island on its east coast. On 23 August it landed near the Moon's south pole, carrying a little rover called Pragyan.

title: The path of the Buddha's teaching
deck: From a garden in Nepal to caves on the Silk Road, a bronze giant in Japan and a stone mountain in Java. Ten places that trace how one teaching crossed Asia.
kidDeck: A teacher called the Buddha lived in northern India about 2,500 years ago. His ideas travelled across the whole of Asia. Follow them to ten famous places.

stops.title: The garden at Lumbini
stops.text: According to sacred texts and Buddhist commentaries, Queen Maya gave birth to Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, at Lumbini around 563 BCE. It is one of the most sacred places of Buddhist pilgrimage. A stone pillar with a Brahmi inscription, found here in 1896, is believed to mark a visit by the emperor Ashoka.
stops.kid: Buddhist tradition says that the Buddha was born here, in a garden called Lumbini in what is now Nepal, about 2,500 years ago. His name then was Siddhartha Gautama.

stops.title: Under the Bodhi Tree
stops.text: Bodh Gaya, in Bihar, is famous as the place where Gautama Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment under what became known as the Bodhi Tree. The first temple on the site was built under the Maurya emperors. The Mahabodhi Temple here became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002.
stops.kid: Buddhists say that at this spot the Buddha sat under a tree and came to understand the truth about life. The tree is called the Bodhi Tree. A great temple stands here now.

stops.title: The first sermon
stops.text: At Sarnath, north-east of Varanasi, the Buddha gave his first sermon after his enlightenment. In 250 BCE the emperor Ashoka raised a column here, topped by a capital of four lions. That Lion Capital is also the State Emblem of India.
stops.kid: At Sarnath the Buddha taught for the first time. About 250 years later the emperor Ashoka put up a tall stone pillar here, with four lions on top. Those four lions are now the symbol of India.

stops.title: The Great Stupa
stops.text: The Great Stupa at Sanchi, on a hilltop in Madhya Pradesh, is one of the oldest stone structures in India. It was commissioned by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE.
stops.kid: This great stone dome on a hill in India is called a stupa. The emperor Ashoka had it built more than 2,200 years ago. It is one of the oldest stone buildings in India.

stops.title: Painted caves
stops.text: At Ajanta in Maharashtra, thirty Buddhist monuments were cut into the rock between the 2nd century BCE and about 480 CE. Their paintings and sculptures are universally regarded as masterpieces of Buddhist religious art. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
stops.kid: Thirty monasteries and prayer halls were cut straight into a cliff here, and the walls were covered with paintings. The paintings are some of the most beautiful Buddhist art in the world.

stops.title: Caves on the Silk Road
stops.text: The teaching travelled with the caravans. Near Dunhuang, an oasis at a crossroads of the Silk Road, the first caves were dug in 366 CE as places of Buddhist meditation and worship. Caves went on being added until the 14th century. In the end there were 500 temples.
stops.kid: Buddhist monks travelled with traders along the Silk Road into China. At a desert oasis they dug caves to pray in, starting in the year 366. Over a thousand years, 500 cave temples were made.

stops.title: The giants of Bamiyan
stops.text: In the Bamiyan Valley of today's Afghanistan, 2,500 metres up, two monumental Buddhas were carved into a cliff. Carbon dating shows the smaller, 38 metres tall, was built around 570 CE. The larger stood 55 metres tall.
stops.kid: In a valley in Afghanistan, two giant statues of the Buddha were carved into a cliff about 1,450 years ago. The bigger one was 55 metres tall.

stops.title: A bronze Buddha in Nara
stops.text: Tōdai-ji, the "Eastern Great Temple", stands in Nara in Japan. Founded in 738 and opened in 752, it was built in imitation of the temples of Tang China. Its Great Buddha Hall houses the world's largest bronze statue of the Buddha.
stops.kid: In the Japanese city of Nara there is a huge temple that opened in the year 752. Inside is the biggest bronze statue of the Buddha in the world.

stops.title: A mountain of stone in Java
stops.text: Borobudur, in Central Java, is a 9th-century Mahayana Buddhist temple built of grey stone during the reign of the Sailendra dynasty. It is decorated with 2,672 relief panels and originally had 504 statues of the Buddha.
stops.kid: On the island of Java in Indonesia stands a temple like a mountain of stone, built about 1,200 years ago. Its walls are covered with 2,672 carved pictures.

stops.title: The palace of the Dalai Lamas
stops.text: The Potala Palace in Lhasa was the winter palace of the Dalai Lamas. The present structure was begun in 1645 on the order of the 5th Dalai Lama. It rises 13 storeys and contains more than 1,000 rooms. Today it is a museum.
stops.kid: High in the mountains of Tibet, in the city of Lhasa, stands a palace with more than a thousand rooms. It was built for the Dalai Lama, the leader of Tibetan Buddhists, starting in 1645.

title: Life's big steps
deck: Ten famous fossil sites, from mats of microbes to footprints in ash. Each pin rides its plate, so you see where the rock was when the creatures were alive.
kidDeck: Rocks keep a diary of life. Visit ten places where amazing fossils were found, from slimy mats of microbes to the footprints of our own ancestors.

stops.title: Rocks built by microbes
stops.text: Stromatolites are layered rock formations built up mainly by photosynthetic microorganisms such as cyanobacteria. They were at their peak about 1.25 billion years ago and later declined. Shark Bay in Western Australia is most renowned for its living stromatolites: hard domes made by colonies of microbial mats, said to be the oldest life forms on Earth.
stops.kid: Long before animals, the sea was full of tiny living things too small to see. Some of them built up layered, bumpy rocks called stromatolites. You can still see living ones today at Shark Bay in Australia.

stops.title: The first big living things
stops.text: At Mistaken Point, on the south-eastern tip of Newfoundland, a rock formation holds one of the most diverse and best preserved collections of Ediacaran fossils. They are the oldest known remnants of multicellular life on Earth.
stops.kid: For a very long time all living things were tiny. The rocks at this spot in Canada hold the oldest known fossils of living things made of many cells.

stops.title: An explosion of animals
stops.text: The Burgess Shale, in the Canadian Rockies near the town of Field in Yoho National Park, dates to about 508 to 505 million years ago. It is famous because it preserved soft-bodied animals, as thin dark films on the rock. The palaeontologist Charles Walcott discovered it on 30 August 1909.
stops.kid: High in the mountains of Canada is a rock full of strange sea animals from 508 million years ago. Even their soft parts were saved, pressed flat like flowers in a book. It was found in 1909.

stops.title: Plants reach the land
stops.text: The Rhynie chert, near a village in Aberdeenshire, formed about 410 million years ago and preserves early land life in extraordinary detail. Most of the fossils are primitive plants, which had water-conducting cells but no true leaves, along with arthropods, lichens, algae and fungi.
stops.kid: Life began in water. This rock in Scotland shows some of the first plants that lived on land, 410 million years ago. They had stems to carry water but no real leaves yet. Small creepy-crawlies lived among them.

stops.title: A fish with a neck
stops.text: Tiktaalik lived about 375 million years ago. It was a lobe-finned fish, with scales and gills, but it had many features of four-legged animals, including a flattened, triangular head. The first fossils were found in 2004 on Ellesmere Island in Arctic Canada.
stops.kid: Tiktaalik was a fish, with scales and gills. But it had a flat, triangular head and unusual fins. It is a clue to how fish slowly became animals with four legs. Its fossils were found in the Arctic in 2004.

stops.title: A coal-age rainforest
stops.text: The cliffs at Joggins in Nova Scotia are famous for their record of a rainforest ecosystem of about 310 million years ago, in the "Coal Age". The fossils are mainly seed ferns, lycopsids and horsetails, with early four-legged animals and sea life. A 15-km stretch of the coast is a World Heritage Site.
stops.kid: These sea cliffs in Canada hold a whole fossil forest from 310 million years ago, the time when coal was made. There are ferns, horsetails and early four-legged animals.

stops.title: Feathers in stone
stops.text: The Solnhofen Limestone of Bavaria is a Jurassic deposit that preserves even soft-bodied creatures such as jellyfish in fine detail. Its most familiar fossils are of Archaeopteryx, an early feathered dinosaur. They are among the most famous and most beautiful fossils in the world.
stops.kid: In the limestone of southern Germany, people found fossils of Archaeopteryx, an early dinosaur with feathers. They are some of the most famous fossils in the world.

stops.title: Fifty-eight kinds of dinosaur
stops.text: In the badlands of Alberta, sediments laid down over about 1.5 million years of the Late Cretaceous have yielded fifty-eight species of dinosaur. More than 500 specimens have been removed and shown in museums around the globe. In all, nearly 500 species of life are known from the park, from fern spores to large carnivorous dinosaurs.
stops.kid: This park in Canada is one of the best places in the world to find dinosaurs. Fossils of 58 different kinds have been dug up here, and they are in museums all over the world.

stops.title: A lake after the dinosaurs
stops.text: The Messel Pit in Hesse dates to about 47 million years ago. Its oil shale, laid down in a lake, is renowned for fossils of plants, arthropods and vertebrates in exceptional preservation. It has given significant evidence about the early evolution of mammals and birds. Once nearly turned into a landfill, it became a World Heritage Site in 1995.
stops.kid: After the dinosaurs died out, mammals and birds took over. At this old lake in Germany, fossils from 47 million years ago are so perfect that they show us how early mammals and birds lived. It was almost turned into a rubbish dump, but people saved it.

stops.title: Footprints in the ash
stops.text: At Laetoli in Tanzania, a trail of footprints dated to 3.7 million years ago is preserved in volcanic ash. Mary Leakey and her team discovered the tracks in 1976. They gave convincing evidence that our relatives of that time already walked upright on two legs.
stops.kid: A long time ago, in Africa, some of our very early relatives walked across fresh ash from a volcano. Their footprints are still there. They show that these early relatives already walked on two legs, like us.

title: Watching the sky
deck: A ring of posts in Germany, thirteen towers in Peru, a stone sundial in Jaipur, sixty-six dishes in a Chilean desert. Eleven places built to watch the sky.
kidDeck: People have always watched the Sun, Moon and stars. Visit eleven places they built to do it, from a wooden circle 7,000 years old to giant telescopes on mountain tops.

stops.title: A circle for the Sun
stops.text: The Goseck Circle in Germany is a Neolithic structure built around 4900 BC and apparently used until about 4700 BC. Its German name calls it a sun observatory. Its ditch, 75 metres across, and two rings of palisades have entrances aligned with sunrise and sunset at the winter solstice.
stops.kid: Almost 7,000 years ago, farmers in what is now Germany built a great circle of wooden posts and ditches. Its gates line up with where the Sun rises and sets on the shortest day of the year.

stops.title: Thirteen towers
stops.text: At Chankillo, in the coastal desert of Peru, a row of thirteen towers runs along a ridge beside a hilltop fort. The Thirteen Towers have been interpreted as an astronomical observatory built in the third century BC.
stops.kid: In the desert of Peru there is a line of thirteen stone towers on a hill. They were built about 2,250 years ago. Seen from the right spot, the Sun rises behind a different tower as the year goes by, like a giant calendar.

stops.title: Maragheh
stops.text: The Maragheh observatory, in today's Iran, was established in the mid 13th century under the patronage of the Ilkhanid ruler Hulagu. Its director was Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, a Persian scientist and astronomer.
stops.kid: In the 1200s a great observatory was built at Maragheh in Persia, now Iran. It was run by a famous Persian astronomer, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. A Mongol ruler paid for it.

stops.title: Kublai Khan's observatory
stops.text: Near Dengfeng in Henan, at a site with a long tradition of sky-watching, a great observatory was built in 1276 on the order of Kublai Khan. The astronomers Guo Shoujing and Wang Xun designed it to observe the movement of the Sun and the stars and to record time.
stops.kid: In 1276 the ruler of China, Kublai Khan, ordered a big observatory to be built. Two astronomers designed it to follow the Sun and the stars and to keep track of time.

stops.title: The prince who mapped the stars
stops.text: In the 1420s the Timurid astronomer Ulugh Beg built an observatory at Samarkand. It was a school of astronomy, and the last of its kind from the medieval Islamic period.
stops.kid: In the city of Samarkand, a ruler and astronomer named Ulugh Beg built an observatory in the 1420s. It was also a school for astronomers.

stops.title: The last observatory without a telescope
stops.text: Uraniborg was built about 1576 to 1580 on the island of Ven by the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe. It was the first custom-built observatory in modern Europe, and the last to be built without a telescope as its main instrument.
stops.kid: On a small island, the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe built an observatory around 1580. It was the last great observatory in Europe built without a telescope.

stops.title: Where time is counted from
stops.text: The Royal Observatory stands on a hill in Greenwich Park in London, above the River Thames. It played a major role in the history of astronomy and navigation. Because the Prime Meridian passed through it, it gave its name to Greenwich Mean Time, the forerunner of today's Coordinated Universal Time.
stops.kid: This observatory in London helped sailors find their way at sea. The line that divides the world's maps into east and west runs right through it, and the world's clocks were once set by its time.

stops.title: Instruments of stone
stops.text: The Jantar Mantar in Jaipur is a collection of 19 astronomical instruments built by the Rajput king Sawai Jai Singh, the founder of the city. It was completed in 1734 and includes the world's largest stone sundial. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
stops.kid: In the Indian city of Jaipur, a king built 19 giant instruments out of stone. One of them is the biggest stone sundial in the world. They were finished in 1734.

stops.title: The biggest eye for thirty years
stops.text: Mount Wilson Observatory sits on a 1,740-metre peak near Pasadena in California. Its 100-inch Hooker telescope was the largest in the world from its completion in 1917 until 1949.
stops.kid: On a mountain in California stands a telescope with a mirror 2.5 metres wide. When it was finished in 1917 it was the biggest in the world, and it stayed the biggest for more than thirty years.

stops.title: A dish in a sinkhole
stops.text: The main instrument of the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico was a spherical reflector dish 305 metres across, built into a natural sinkhole. Its receiver hung 150 metres above the dish on cables. Completed in 1963, it was the world's largest single-aperture telescope for 53 years.
stops.kid: In Puerto Rico, a giant dish 305 metres wide was built in a natural hollow in the hills. For 53 years it was the biggest single telescope dish in the world.

stops.title: Sixty-six dishes in the desert
stops.text: ALMA is an array of 66 radio telescopes working as one, on a plateau 5,000 metres up in the Atacama Desert of Chile. It began observing in 2011 and has been fully operational since March 2013. Like the observatories on Mauna Kea in Hawaii, at 4,207 metres, it sits high to get above most of the water vapour in the air.
stops.kid: High in a desert in Chile, 66 radio dishes work together like one enormous telescope. They are 5,000 metres up, where the air is thin and dry and the view of space is very clear.

title: Building big
deck: Stone pillars raised by people who did not farm, a tomb that took 26 years, a dome that was the world's largest room, a canal that cut a continent in two. Thirteen things people built to last.
kidDeck: People have always loved to build something huge. Visit thirteen giant buildings, from stone circles made before farming to the tallest tower in the world.

stops.title: The oldest great stones
stops.text: Göbekli Tepe, in today's Turkey, was inhabited from around 9500 BCE to at least 8000 BCE. It is known for large circular structures holding massive stone pillars, among the world's oldest known megaliths. Many pillars carry reliefs of wild animals.
stops.kid: More than 11,000 years ago, people raised rings of giant stone pillars on a hill in what is now Turkey, and carved wild animals on them. They are some of the oldest big stone monuments in the world.

stops.title: Stonehenge
stops.text: Stonehenge, on Salisbury Plain in England, was built in several phases beginning about 3100 BC. Its outer ring is of standing stones about four metres high, each weighing around 25 tons. The whole monument is aligned towards sunrise on the summer solstice and sunset on the winter solstice.
stops.kid: Stonehenge is a ring of huge standing stones in England, begun about 5,000 years ago. Each big stone weighs about 25 tons. The stones line up with the sunrise on the longest day of the year.

stops.title: The Great Pyramid
stops.text: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the largest of the Egyptian pyramids, built about 2600 BC over a period of about 26 years as the tomb of the pharaoh Khufu. It first stood 146.6 metres high. It is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and the only one that remains largely intact.
stops.kid: The Great Pyramid in Egypt was built about 4,600 years ago as a tomb for a king named Khufu. It took about 26 years to build and was 146 metres tall. It is the only one of the seven wonders of the ancient world still standing.

stops.title: The first walls of the Great Wall
stops.text: The Great Wall of China is not one wall but a series of fortifications, built across the northern borders of Chinese states and empires as protection against nomadic groups from the Eurasian Steppe. The first walls date to the 7th century BC. Later rulers joined them together.
stops.kid: The Great Wall of China is really many walls, built over a very long time to keep out raiders from the north. The first parts were built about 2,700 years ago.

stops.title: Water over a river
stops.text: The Pont du Gard is a Roman aqueduct bridge in southern France, built in the first century AD. It was part of a channel that carried water more than 50 km to the Roman town of Nemausus, today's Nîmes. It is one of the best preserved Roman aqueduct bridges.
stops.kid: The Romans built this tall bridge in France almost 2,000 years ago. It carried water, in a channel more than 50 kilometres long, to a Roman town.

stops.title: The Pantheon
stops.text: The Pantheon in Rome was a temple "of all the gods", first built under the emperor Augustus and reconstructed under Hadrian, who reigned from 117 to 138. Since AD 609 it has served as a church.
stops.kid: The Pantheon in Rome was built as a temple to all the Roman gods. The building you can see today was rebuilt by the emperor Hadrian almost 1,900 years ago. Today it is used as a church.

stops.title: The largest room in the world
stops.text: Hagia Sophia in Istanbul was completed in AD 537, the last of three churches built on the site by the Eastern Roman Empire. It became the world's largest interior space, and was among the first buildings to use a fully pendentive dome. It was a church until 1453, later a museum, and is now a mosque.
stops.kid: When Hagia Sophia was finished in the year 537, it was the biggest indoor space in the world, under a giant dome. It was a church for centuries, later a museum, and is a mosque today.

stops.title: The temple city of Angkor
stops.text: Angkor Wat in Cambodia was constructed between 1113 and 1150 during the reign of the Khmer king Suryavarman II, as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu. It later became a Buddhist temple. Its site covers 162.6 hectares, and it is the largest religious complex in the world.
stops.kid: Angkor Wat in Cambodia is the biggest religious building in the world. A Khmer king had it built about 900 years ago as a Hindu temple. Later it became a Buddhist temple.

stops.title: Great Zimbabwe: walls without mortar
stops.text: Great Zimbabwe, in the south-eastern hills of today's Zimbabwe, was settled from around 1000 AD and was the capital of a kingdom from the 13th century. It is the largest stone structure in precolonial Southern Africa. The dry stone walls of its Great Enclosure, 11 metres high, were built without mortar in the 13th and 14th centuries.
stops.kid: Great Zimbabwe was a city of stone in southern Africa, the capital of a kingdom about 800 years ago. Its great walls, 11 metres high, were built of stone without any mortar to hold them together.

stops.title: A citadel in the clouds
stops.text: Machu Picchu is an Inca citadel on a mountain ridge 2,430 metres up in the Andes of Peru. It is estimated to have been built around 1450 and is believed to have been an estate of the Inca emperor Pachacuti, though no written record of the time confirms it. It was abandoned roughly a century later.
stops.kid: High on a mountain ridge in Peru, the Inca built a town of stone around the year 1450. It was probably a home for the emperor. About a hundred years later it was left empty.

stops.title: The Taj Mahal
stops.text: The Taj Mahal is an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the bank of the river Yamuna in Agra. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan commissioned it in 1631 to house the tomb of his late wife, Mumtaz Mahal. The mausoleum was completed in 1648. It also holds the tomb of Shah Jahan himself.
stops.kid: The emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in India as a tomb for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal. It is made of white marble and was finished in 1648. The emperor is buried there too.

stops.title: A shortcut between two seas
stops.text: The Suez Canal is an artificial sea-level waterway through Egypt, joining the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. The French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps formed a company to build it in 1858. Construction lasted from 1859 to 1869, and the canal officially opened on 17 November 1869.
stops.kid: In 1869 a canal was opened through Egypt, joining two seas. It gave ships a direct route between Europe and Asia. It took ten years to dig.

stops.title: The tallest tower
stops.text: The Burj Khalifa in Dubai is the world's tallest structure, with a total height of 829.8 metres. Construction began in 2004, and it has been the tallest building in the world since its inauguration. The iron Eiffel Tower in Paris, for comparison, was built by Gustave Eiffel's company from 1887 to 1889.
stops.kid: The Burj Khalifa in Dubai is the tallest building in the world: almost 830 metres high. Work on it started in 2004.

title: Battles that changed the map
deck: Chariots at Kadesh, citizens at Marathon, cannon at Constantinople and Panipat, a mountain valley in Vietnam. Fourteen battles after which the world was arranged differently.
kidDeck: Sadly, wars have shaped a lot of history. Visit fourteen battlefields and find out who fought there, and what changed afterwards.

stops.title: Kadesh: five thousand chariots
stops.text: In the early 13th century BC, Ramesses II of Egypt attacked the Hittite Empire of Muwatalli II on the Orontes River. It is the earliest pitched battle for which details of tactics and formations are known, and is believed to be the largest chariot battle ever fought, with 5,000 to 6,000 chariots in all.
stops.kid: More than 3,200 years ago, the armies of Egypt and the Hittites fought beside a river on what is today the border of Lebanon and Syria. Thousands of chariots took part. It is the oldest battle that we know the details of.

stops.title: Marathon
stops.text: In 490 BCE the citizens of Athens, aided by Plataea, met a Persian force sent by King Darius I in his first attempt to subjugate Greece. The Greek army inflicted a crushing defeat on the more numerous Persians. It was a turning point in the Greco-Persian Wars.
stops.kid: In 490 BCE the huge Persian Empire sent an army to conquer Greece. The citizens of Athens met it at a place called Marathon and won, even though there were more Persians.

stops.title: Gaugamela
stops.text: In 331 BC the army of Macedon under Alexander the Great met the Persian army of King Darius III. It was the second and final battle between the two kings. Alexander's decisive victory led to the fall of the Achaemenid Empire.
stops.kid: In 331 BC Alexander the Great fought the Persian king Darius III for the last time, in what is now Iraq. Alexander won, and the great Persian Empire fell.

stops.title: Cannae
stops.text: On 2 August 216 BC, near the village of Cannae in south-east Italy, the Carthaginians and their allies under Hannibal surrounded and practically annihilated a larger Roman army. It was a key engagement of the Second Punic War between Rome and Carthage.
stops.kid: Hannibal was a general from the city of Carthage. In 216 BC, in Italy, his army surrounded a bigger Roman army and destroyed almost all of it.

stops.title: Red Cliffs
stops.text: In the winter of 208 to 209 AD, at the end of the Han dynasty, a decisive naval battle was fought on the Yangtze River. The allied forces of Sun Quan, Liu Bei and Liu Qi, based south of the river, defeated the numerically superior forces of the northern warlord Cao Cao.
stops.kid: In the winter of the year 208, warlords fought a great battle with ships on the Yangtze River in China. The smaller side won, and the northern warlord Cao Cao could not conquer the south.

stops.title: Tours
stops.text: On 10 October 732, during the Umayyad invasion of Gaul, Frankish and Aquitanian forces defeated the invading army. In Arabic it is remembered as the Battle of the Highway of the Martyrs.
stops.kid: In the year 732 an army from the Umayyad Caliphate marched into what is now France. The Franks defeated it. The battle is named after the city of Tours.

stops.title: Ain Jalut
stops.text: On 3 September 1260, near the spring of Ain Jalut in the Jezreel Valley, the Mamluks of Egypt fought the Mongols of the Ilkhanate. The battle marks the first major halt to the Mongol advance.
stops.kid: In 1260 the army of Egypt, the Mamluks, fought the Mongols at a spring called Ain Jalut. It was the first time the Mongol advance was really stopped.

stops.title: The fall of Constantinople
stops.text: After a 53-day siege that began on 6 April, the Ottoman army of Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire, on 29 May 1453. The attackers greatly outnumbered the defenders. The fall marked the effective end of the Roman Empire, a state that had lasted nearly 1,500 years.
stops.kid: Constantinople was the capital of the last part of the old Roman Empire. In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II surrounded the city for 53 days and then captured it. The Roman Empire, almost 1,500 years old, was over.

stops.title: Panipat
stops.text: On 21 April 1526 the invading forces of Babur met the army of Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi. Babur's forces, using gunpowder firearms and cannons, won. It was one of the earliest battles with gunpowder arms on the Indian subcontinent.
stops.kid: In 1526 a ruler named Babur invaded northern India. At Panipat his army used guns and cannons, which were new in India, and defeated the Sultan of Delhi.

stops.title: Plassey
stops.text: On 23 June 1757 the British East India Company under Robert Clive won a decisive victory over the Nawab of Bengal and his French allies. The victory was made possible by the betrayal of Mir Jafar, commander in chief of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah, and of much of the Bengal army.
stops.kid: In 1757 a British trading company fought the ruler of Bengal, in India. The company won because the ruler's own general, Mir Jafar, betrayed him.

stops.title: Waterloo
stops.text: On Sunday 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in today's Belgium, the French army of Napoleon I was defeated by two armies of the Seventh Coalition, one of them British-led under the Duke of Wellington. It was Napoleon's last engagement.
stops.kid: On 18 June 1815, at Waterloo in Belgium, Napoleon, the emperor of France, fought his last battle and lost.

stops.title: Adwa
stops.text: On 1 March 1896, near the town of Adwa, the Ethiopian Empire under Emperor Menelik II met an Italian colonial force. The battle ended in a decisive Ethiopian victory, and forced Italy to recognise Ethiopia's sovereignty in the Treaty of Addis Ababa.
stops.kid: In 1896 Italy tried to take over Ethiopia. At Adwa the Ethiopian army, led by Emperor Menelik II, won a great victory. Italy had to accept that Ethiopia was a free country.

stops.title: Stalingrad
stops.text: From August 1942 Nazi Germany and its allies fought the Soviet Union for the city of Stalingrad, now Volgograd, in close-quarters combat and with heavy civilian losses under aerial bombardment. The Soviet victory, complete by 2 February 1943, is generally regarded as the pivotal turning point of the war in Europe.
stops.kid: In the Second World War, the German and Soviet armies fought for months over the city of Stalingrad, street by street. The Soviet side won in February 1943. After that, Germany was pushed back.

stops.title: Dien Bien Phu
stops.text: Between 13 March and 7 May 1954 the Viet Minh besieged French forces at Điện Biên Phủ, in the north-west of Vietnam. After two months the garrison was overrun and the survivors surrendered. The defeat led to the gradual withdrawal of French forces from Indochina.
stops.kid: In 1954 Vietnamese fighters called the Viet Minh surrounded a French army base for two months and captured it. After that, French forces gradually left the region.

title: India's road to freedom
deck: From a mutiny in Meerut in 1857 to a midnight speech in Delhi in 1947. Eleven places on the ninety-year road to Indian independence.
kidDeck: For a long time Britain ruled India. Follow eleven steps on the road to freedom, from a soldiers' revolt in 1857 to the midnight when India became independent.

stops.title: The rebellion begins
stops.text: On 10 May 1857 the sepoys, the Indian soldiers, of the East India Company's garrison at Meerut mutinied. It was the start of a major uprising in 1857 and 1858 against the Company, which ruled India as a sovereign power on behalf of the British Crown.
stops.kid: A British company ruled most of India, using Indian soldiers. On 10 May 1857 the soldiers at Meerut rebelled. The revolt spread and lasted more than a year.

stops.title: A congress is founded
stops.text: The Indian National Congress was founded on 28 December 1885 and held its first session that year in Bombay, today's Mumbai. It was the first modern nationalist movement to emerge in the non-European British Empire.
stops.kid: In December 1885 the Indian National Congress was founded. It held its first meeting in Bombay. It was the first modern movement of its kind in the British Empire outside Europe.

stops.title: Gandhi's first satyagraha
stops.text: In 1917, in the Champaran district of Bihar, farmers rose in protest at being made to grow indigo for barely any payment. It was the first satyagraha movement led by Mahatma Gandhi in British India. He had returned from South Africa in 1915.
stops.kid: Farmers in Champaran were forced to grow a plant called indigo, and were paid almost nothing. In 1917 Mahatma Gandhi came to help them. It was his first peaceful protest in India.

stops.title: Jallianwala Bagh
stops.text: On 13 April 1919 a large crowd gathered at the Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, during the Baisakhi fair, to protest against the Rowlatt Act and the arrest of independence activists. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer blocked the exit with his troops and ordered them to shoot at the crowd. Estimates of those killed vary from 379 to 1,500 or more, and over 1,200 others were injured.
stops.kid: On 13 April 1919 a big crowd met in a garden in Amritsar to protest. A British general blocked the way out and ordered his soldiers to shoot. Between 379 and 1,500 people, or more, were killed.

stops.title: Chauri Chaura
stops.text: On 4 February 1922 at Chauri Chaura, police fired on a large group of protesters taking part in the non-cooperation movement. In retaliation the demonstrators attacked and set fire to a police station. Three civilians and 22 policemen died. Gandhi halted the movement.
stops.kid: In 1922 a protest turned violent. Police shot at the protesters, and the protesters burned down a police station. People died on both sides. After this, Gandhi stopped the whole campaign.

stops.title: The Kakori train action
stops.text: On 9 August 1925, at Kakori, a village near Lucknow, revolutionaries of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association robbed a train.
stops.kid: In 1925 a group of revolutionaries robbed a train at Kakori, near Lucknow, as part of the struggle against British rule.

stops.title: The Salt March
stops.text: In 1930 the Indian National Congress passed the Purna Swaraj resolution, a declaration of complete independence. That spring Gandhi led the 24-day Salt March, 387 km from Sabarmati Ashram to the sea at Dandi, where on 6 April he broke the British salt laws. Millions of Indians followed with civil disobedience of their own.
stops.kid: In 1930 Gandhi walked 387 kilometres to the sea and made salt, which was against British law. Millions of Indians then broke the salt law too.

stops.title: Quit India
stops.text: On 8 August 1942, during the Second World War, Gandhi launched the Quit India Movement at the Bombay session of the All India Congress Committee. In his speech at the Gowalia Tank Maidan he made a call to "Do or Die", demanding an end to British rule.
stops.kid: On 8 August 1942, in Bombay, Gandhi told the British it was time to leave India. "Do or die," he told the crowd.

stops.title: The navy rises
stops.text: In February 1946 Indian sailors of the Royal Indian Navy rose against the British government in India. From its flashpoint in Bombay the revolt spread from Karachi to Calcutta, and came to involve over 10,000 sailors in 56 ships and shore establishments. It failed, but it found support across British India.
stops.kid: In February 1946 Indian sailors in the navy refused to obey their British officers. It began in Bombay and spread to 56 ships and bases. The revolt was put down, but people all over India supported it.

stops.title: Midnight
stops.text: India and Pakistan legally came into existence at midnight on 14–15 August 1947. Towards midnight Jawaharlal Nehru, the first Prime Minister of India, gave his "Tryst with Destiny" speech to the Constituent Assembly in Parliament House. British India had been divided in two. The partition displaced between 12 and 20 million people along religious lines.
stops.kid: At midnight on 14 August 1947, India became a free country. Its first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, gave a famous speech in Delhi. But British India was split into two countries, India and Pakistan. Between 12 and 20 million people had to leave their homes.

stops.title: A constitution
stops.text: The Constitution of India is the supreme legal document of India, and the longest written national constitution in the world. The Constituent Assembly of India adopted it on 26 November 1949, and it became effective on 26 January 1950. It sets out the framework of government along with fundamental rights and directive principles.
stops.kid: A free country needs rules that everyone, even the government, must follow. India's rule book is called the Constitution. It is the longest written constitution of any country in the world.

title: Who counts? The widening circle of rights
deck: A charter sealed in a meadow, a declaration in Paris, a revolt of the enslaved, a petition in New Zealand, a bus in Alabama, a queue of first-time voters in South Africa. Eleven steps, none of them the last.
kidDeck: Once, only kings and a few rich men had rights. Visit eleven places where people fought for fairer rules, so that more and more people were counted.

stops.title: A king agrees to rules
stops.text: On 15 June 1215, in a water-meadow beside the Thames at Runnymede, King John of England sealed Magna Carta, the "Great Charter". It was drafted to make peace between an unpopular king and a group of rebel barons, and promised, among other things, protection for the barons from illegal imprisonment.
stops.kid: In 1215 the powerful lords of England forced King John to agree to a list of rules, called Magna Carta. It promised that the lords could not be locked up illegally.

stops.title: A declaration in Philadelphia
stops.text: On 4 July 1776 the Second Continental Congress unanimously adopted the Declaration of Independence, the founding document of the United States. It was debated and adopted at what is now called Independence Hall in Philadelphia, where the Constitution of the United States was later adopted too.
stops.kid: On 4 July 1776, in a hall in the city of Philadelphia, thirteen colonies in North America declared their independence. That was the birth of the United States.

stops.title: The rights of man
stops.text: In 1789, during the French Revolution, France's National Constituent Assembly set out the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, a document of human and civil rights. The Marquis de Lafayette prepared the first drafts, in consultation with Thomas Jefferson. Most of the final text came from the Abbé Sieyès.
stops.kid: In 1789, during the French Revolution, the new French assembly wrote down a list of rights that belong to every citizen.

sources.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

stops.title: The enslaved free themselves
stops.text: In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, enslaved Black Africans rose against colonial rule on 21 August 1791. The struggle ended with independence on 1 January 1804. Their revolution is one of the only known slave rebellions in history that led to the founding of a state both free from slavery and ruled by people who had been enslaved. That state is Haiti.
stops.kid: On a Caribbean island ruled by France, enslaved people rose up and fought for their freedom. They won, and founded their own country, Haiti.

stops.title: Britain abolishes slavery
stops.text: The Slavery Abolition Act of 1833, passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom, abolished slavery in the British Empire. It did so by way of what was called compensated emancipation.
stops.kid: In 1833 the British Parliament passed a law ending slavery in the British Empire.

stops.title: A convention for women's rights
stops.text: On 19 and 20 July 1848 the first women's rights convention met in the Wesleyan Chapel at Seneca Falls, New York. Its organisers advertised it as "a convention to discuss the social, civil, and religious condition and rights of woman".
stops.kid: In 1848, in a small town called Seneca Falls, people held the first big meeting about women's rights.

stops.title: Emancipation
stops.text: On 1 January 1863, in the middle of the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation. It changed the legal status of more than 3.5 million enslaved African Americans in the Confederate states.
stops.kid: On 1 January 1863, during a civil war in the United States, President Abraham Lincoln announced that more than 3.5 million enslaved people in the states that had broken away were to be free.

stops.title: Every woman can vote
stops.text: After years of campaigning led by Kate Sheppard, who organised the Women's Suffrage Petition of 1893, New Zealand became the first nation in the world in which all women had the right to vote in parliamentary elections.
stops.kid: In 1893 New Zealand became the first country in the world where all women could vote. A woman named Kate Sheppard led the campaign and organised a great petition.

stops.title: Rights for all human beings
stops.text: On 10 December 1948, meeting at the Palais de Chaillot in Paris, the United Nations General Assembly accepted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It was drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, and sets out rights and freedoms of all human beings.
stops.kid: After the Second World War, the countries of the United Nations agreed on a list of rights that every single person in the world should have. They accepted it in Paris on 10 December 1948.

stops.title: A seat on the bus
stops.text: On 5 December 1955, the Monday after Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her seat to a white person, Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama began a boycott of the city's segregated buses. It lasted until 20 December 1956 and was a foundational event of the civil rights movement. On 28 August 1963, at the March on Washington, Martin Luther King Jr. gave his "I Have a Dream" speech in front of the Lincoln Memorial.
stops.kid: In Montgomery, Black people had to give up their bus seats to white people. In 1955 Rosa Parks refused, and was arrested. For more than a year, Black people in the city refused to ride the buses at all, until the rule was changed.

stops.title: Everyone votes
stops.text: Between 26 and 29 April 1994 South Africa held the first election in which citizens of all races could vote, the country's first under universal suffrage. The African National Congress won 62 percent of the vote. The pin is on Pretoria, the administrative capital.
stops.kid: In April 1994, for the first time, South Africans of all races could vote in an election.
